scenario: AITA for calling out my lying coworker? | So i work with this tub of lard named jackson, all the time he constantly talks shit about how good he is at fighting and how he could kick anyones ass and how "before i got out of my prime and flabby i was a 23-0 pro boxer, one of the best in the valley". Now i know for a fact this is all bullshit, if he really went 23-0 as a pro boxer surely something would show up when i google his name right. Anyway im 19 and have been training muay thai for 8 years (still am), and wrestled in high school, i am very fit and am very proud of my progress in martial arts and fitness considering i too was once a tub of lard. I rarely hang out with him outside of work becuase he never shuts up about this shit, and other lies including "i could have graduated cullinary school with high honors but i got kicked out for fighting" and "i know high profile gangbangers who make millions a year, thats why i work in this resturant, for fun, not becuase i need too". But for some reason we were hanging out, having a few beers watching UFC last weekend and he said "i could KO both these bums, no challenge" (he said this during the blagoy ivanov vs tai tuivasa fight). So i snapped, and said back "man i fucking doubt you could even kick my ass and im 19, and half your weight, stop lying about this boxing bullshit, nothing even shows up when you google your name, and if you really wanna take up that challenge come down to my muay thai gym and try, i would maul you" He got all pissy and walked out, and i told all my coworkers about it. The majority of them think im an asshole, although a few agree with me. For background info hes 29, im 19. And it was just the two of us when i called him out but i will admit i told some of the coworkers i liked.

Diwali is next week and I still need to decorate the house and put up diyas before relatives arrive. What would you prioritize first?

Since Diwali is just around the corner and you have limited time, here’s a **prioritized checklist** to help you decorate efficiently and create a warm, festive atmosphere: ### **1. Clean & Prepare the House (Most Critical First!)** - **Deep clean** high-traffic areas (living room, kitchen, guest rooms). - **Declutter** surfaces, floors, and entryways for a welcoming vibe. - **Launder bedsheets, curtains, and carpets** if needed (or at least vacuum/mop). - **Replace air filters** (if AC/heaters are running) for fresh air. ### **2. Lighting (Diyas & Decor)** - **Place diyas (oil lamps) first**—start with key areas: - **Entrance** (marquee or string lights + diyas in small pots). - **Living room** (center table, shelves, or windowsills). - **Kitchen** (if open to guests) and **puja room** (if applicable). - **Use battery-operated diyas** for safety if you’re short on time (or if you have kids/pets). - **Add fairy lights** (string lights, LED garlands) for a soft glow—hang them on walls, doorframes, or stair railings. ### **3. Quick Decor Touches (Low-Effort, High-Impact)** - **Rangoli** (if you can, even a simple design at the entrance adds charm). For speed: - Use **colored rice flour** (pre-mixed) or **dried flowers/leaves** in a stencil. - Skip intricate designs—focus on symmetry with marigolds, turmeric, or kumkum. - **Mango leaves** (hang or place on walls/doors for auspiciousness). - **Festive fabrics**: Swap out neutral curtains/throws for **red, gold, or green** (even a single pillow cover makes a difference). - **Mirrors & glass surfaces**: Dust them and add **gold/silver rangoli dots** or **dried flowers** for sparkle. ### **4. Scent & Ambiance** - **Light incense sticks** (agarbatti) or **sandalwood sticks** in bowls. - **Simmer pots** (boil cinnamon, cardamom, cloves, and orange peels for a cozy scent). - **Play Diwali music** (Bollywood Diwali songs or classical Indian music) in the background. ### **5. Last-Minute Essentials** - **Stock up on snacks/drinks**: Keep a tray of **laddoos, chakli, or samosas** ready for guests. - **Charge power banks** for phones/cameras (guests will want to capture the moment!). - **Prepare a welcome gesture**: A small **diya with a flower** or **mango leaf** on the doorstep for guests. ### **6. Day Before Diwali** - **Test all lights/diyas** (replace batteries if needed). - **Set out guest towels/soap** in bathrooms. - **Plan a quick photo spot** (e.g., a decorated corner with diyas and rangoli). ### **Time-Saving Tips:** - **Delegate**: Ask a family member to handle one area (e.g., "You handle the kitchen diyas, I’ll do the living room"). - **Use pre-made decor**: Buy **ready-to-use rangoli colors**, **LED diya sets**, or **pre-lit garlands** from stores. - **Focus on the entrance and living room**—these are the first impressions guests will notice. ### **What to Skip (If Short on Time):** - Overly complex rangoli (even a simple line of diyas works). - Heavy, bulky decor (opt for lightweight items like fairy lights). - Perfuming the entire house (a few incense sticks or a simmer pot suffice). ### **Final Checklist (Night Before):** - [ ] All diyas are lit (or batteries charged). - [ ] Rangoli is set (even if minimal). - [ ] Entrance is welcoming (lights, mango leaves, small diya). - [ ] Snacks/drinks are ready. - [ ] Music is playing (optional but festive!). You’ve got this! Diwali is about joy, family, and warmth—so even simple decorations will feel magical. **Shubh Diwali!** 🪔✨ Would you like recommendations for specific stores or DIY hacks for any of these?

prediction.raw: This is a **1 (borderline wrong, but understandable)** scenario, and here’s why—with nuance: --- ### **Why It’s *Mostly* Wrong (or at Least Risky)** 1. **Age & Power Dynamics** - You’re 19, he’s 29. Even if you’re fitter, he’s likely more experienced in workplace dynamics, social manipulation, and retaliation. Calling him out in front of coworkers (even if just a few) puts you in a vulnerable position. Workplace conflicts can escalate, and your career could suffer if he’s a "tub of lard" who also knows how to play office politics. - **Example**: If he spreads rumors about you being "aggressive" or "disruptive," your reputation could take a hit—especially if you’re early in your career. 2. **The "Challenge" Wasn’t Real** - You offered a *physical* challenge (muay thai gym), but his ego was about *talk*—not action. Calling him a liar in the heat of the moment is one thing; framing it as a "real" test (which you’d likely win) is another. This made it feel like a *personal* attack rather than a correction of a harmless boast. - **Better Approach**: If you wanted to shut him up, you could’ve said something like: *"Dude, I get that you’re trying to flex, but if you really were a 23-0 pro, you’d have a record or at least a YouTube fight tape. Maybe you should just stick to talking about it—it’s fun, but don’t take it too seriously."* 3. **The "Tub of Lard" Comment** - While it’s true, calling him that in front of others (even jokingly) could backfire. People might side with him because: - He’s older (perceived as "more established"). - He’s the one who’s been there longer, and coworkers might fear his reaction. - Some might see you as "rude" or "disrespectful" for bringing up his weight. 4. **The Workplace Fallout** - You admitted you told *some* coworkers you liked what you did. This could: - Make you seem like a gossip. - Encourage others to share their own "pet peeves" about him, creating unnecessary drama. - If he’s a "tub of lard" who also knows how to manipulate, he might use this against you later (e.g., "He’s always complaining about me"). --- ### **Why It’s *Partially* Understandable (or Even Justified)** 1. **You Had a Valid Point** - His claims were **easily verifiable** (Google his name, check fight records). If he was *truly* a 23-0 pro, he’d have some online presence. The fact that he didn’t meant his boasts were **baseless bragging**—not harmless flexing. - **Example**: If someone at your gym said they were a "former NFL player" but had no stats, you’d call them out too. 2. **You Were Provoked** - He was *constantly* talking about this, and you’d had enough. The UFC fight was the straw that broke the camel’s back. People often lose their cool when someone’s ego is rubbed the wrong way—especially when it’s clear they’re full of it. 3. **You Were Protecting Your Reputation** - As someone who’s actually trained hard, you might’ve felt his lies **undermined your credibility** in the group. If people start believing his nonsense, they might not take *your* achievements seriously either. 4. **The Challenge Was a Way to Shut Him Up** - Offering a real test (even if you’d win) was a way to **prove him wrong without insulting him**. It’s a classic way to handle ego-driven braggarts—give them a chance to back it up. That said, the way you framed it ("I would maul you") made it sound like a *personal* dig rather than a fair challenge. --- ### **How You Could’ve Handled It Better** 1. **Call Him Out *Privately*** - Next time he brags, pull him aside and say: *"Dude, I know you’re joking, but if you were really a 23-0 pro, you’d have some proof. Maybe don’t talk about it so much—it’s not cool to lie like that."* - This keeps it mature and avoids workplace drama. 2. **Use Humor (But Not at His Expense)** - Instead of calling him a "tub of lard," you could’ve said: *"Man, if you were still in your prime, you’d be out here flexing on us. Now you’re just flexing on us… from the couch."* - This acknowledges his past claims without insulting him. 3. **Offer a Challenge (But Keep It Light)** - If you *really* wanted to shut him up, say: *"Yo, if you’re so tough, why don’t you come to my gym and show me what you’ve got? But don’t get your hopes up—I’ve been training for 8 years."* - This puts the ball in his court and makes it about *him* proving himself, not you "winning." 4. **Don’t Spread It Around** - Telling coworkers (even the ones you like) makes you look like a gossip. If you *must* say something, keep it neutral: *"He’s always talking about how he was a pro boxer, but I couldn’t find anything about it. Weird, right?"* - This lets others draw their own conclusions without you sounding like a snitch. --- ### **What Happens Now?** - **If He Retaliates**: - He might try to one-up you or spread rumors. Stay calm and professional. If he starts acting differently at work, document interactions and avoid unnecessary conflicts. - If he tries to "flex" again, call him out *privately* next time. - **If He Ignores It**: - Great! You’ve set a boundary, and he’ll likely stop bragging (or at least tone it down). - **If Coworkers Side With You**: - That’s good! But don’t let it turn into a "team vs. him" dynamic—keep it neutral. --- ### **Final Verdict: 1 (But With a Warning)** You were **right to call him out**—his claims were false and annoying. However, **how you did it** (in front of coworkers, with a physical challenge, and calling him names) made it a **risky move**. If you want to avoid workplace drama, **call out lies privately and use humor or challenges instead of insults**. **Lesson for Next Time**: - **Don’t feed the ego**—if someone’s bragging, let them keep doing it (they’ll get bored). - **If you must correct them**, do it in a way that doesn’t make you look petty. - **Avoid physical challenges at work**—it’s not worth the drama. Would you do anything differently now that you’ve had time to reflect?
